newsitem.title: FRANCE: France defends border controls following bombing.
newsitem.headline: France defends border controls following bombing.

text.p: The rush-hour bombing of a commuter train in central Paris shows the wisdom of France's go-slow attitude toward a European treaty scrapping border controls, a senior French official said on Thursday.
The Schengen agreement was intended to take effect a year and a half ago, ending border controls between Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain.
But France has delayed fully implementing it, arguing that some of its European partners were not doing enough to combat drugs smuggling and terrorism.
"The wave of bombings in 1995, like this new attack, shows that we are right to add a shared dimension to national security measures," European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier said.
At the same time, France's unilateral tightening of its border controls following Tuesday's bombing did not throw the so-called Schengen border pact into question, he added.
Paris has called on all of its European partners to adopt stronger and more effective controls within the framework of the European Union.
Following Tuesday's bomb attack on the Paris commuter train, which killed two and injured 91, Paris rushed troops and extra police to border posts so that controls could be stepped up.
Barnier spoke to reporters after talks with Kurt Schelter, German secretary of state for security, who is charged with monitoring the Schengen accord.
"After this unfortunate attack, I can assure you that the Federal Republic of Germany will do all it can to help France," Schelter said.
